projects.title: EcoCraft
projects.blurb: A website that connects Belfast's local artisans with buyers, built around pop-up markets in unused spaces.
projects.meta: Group project with Katie, Shiva and Laura, 2025. UX research, prototyping and web design.
projects.overview: EcoCraft is an e-commerce website for local artisans in Belfast. The idea is to hold art events and markets in unused or run-down spaces, then let artisans sell online through their own profiles. It was a group project for UXD700, Exploration and Enquiry, submitted in January 2025.

sections.heading: The problem
sections.text: Local artists told us their biggest struggle is getting seen. Many sell mostly through social media, compete with sellers offering the same product, and have few ways to reach a wider audience. Meanwhile, public money has been spent on land that sits unused. We asked: how might we create a marketspace that helps local artisans sell their products sustainably and strengthens community connections in Belfast?

sections.heading: Research
sections.text: We surveyed artisans and customers, and also sent a survey to Belfast City Council about using empty spaces, though we never heard back. Most artisans were comfortable with online platforms and with QR codes at a market. Ninety-one percent of customers were comfortable scanning QR codes, and they said good photos, full product descriptions and easy access matter most on a website. We also looked at existing markets and online sellers, including St George's Market, Wolf and Badger, Craft NI and The Market Co.

sections.heading: Who it's for
sections.text: We worked from two personas, Claire, a ceramic potter who wants a wider audience and less admin, and David, a sustainability-minded buyer who struggles to find local makers. Empathy maps and journey maps for both showed the same gap: people meet at a market, but there is nothing to carry that connection online afterwards.

sections.heading: The solution
sections.text: Customers see something they like at a market, scan a QR code, and land on the artisan's profile to browse and buy. Artisans create a profile, list products and promote events, and can switch between buyer and seller views. The site also has search, an events page, reviews and a wishlist. We went from paper sketches to a low fidelity prototype, then a final design in a green palette chosen to suit the sustainable focus.

sections.heading: Sustainability
sections.text: Artisans carry less stock to each market, since buyers can order the rest online. Digital promotion replaces flyers, and reusing empty spaces avoids new building. The project links to four UN Sustainable Development Goals: 8, 11, 12 and 13.

sections.heading: What we didn't get to
sections.text: We ran out of time to test the website with real users, so the design is untested. That would be the next step, along with a reply from the Council about the spaces.

projects.title: Food Delivery App
projects.blurb: A food ordering app that gets a meal from menu to doorstep in five screens. Warm neutrals and one dark accent let the food photography stay the loudest thing on screen.
projects.meta: Concept project, 2026. UX design, UI design and mobile app.
projects.overview: A food ordering app that gets a meal from menu to doorstep in five screens. Warm neutrals and one dark accent let the food photography stay the loudest thing on screen.

sections.heading: The challenge
sections.text: Ordering apps tend to bury the decision under banners, offers and nested menus. The aim here was a flow where a hungry person can pick a meal, see exactly what it costs and know when it arrives, with no detours.

sections.heading: The approach
sections.text: Two menu screens feed one bag, and from there the path is a straight line: review, pay, confirm. Each menu card shows a photo, name, calories, a one line description and the price, so you can add a meal straight from the list. A floating tab bar keeps Quick Bites, Healthy Diet and Desserts one tap apart.

sections.heading: Checkout
sections.text: Checkout opens with the delivery address, a mapped route and a 15 minute estimate. Meal, tax, delivery and promo discount are itemised above the total, and the pay button repeats the final amount.

sections.heading: Order confirmation
sections.text: The confirmation screen shows who's delivering (name, vehicle plate, message and call shortcuts), when they'll arrive and where they're going. It ends on one action: Track Your Order.

sections.heading: Visual design
sections.text: Five colours: cream background, sand cards, tan image tiles, cocoa for buttons and the tab bar, and black for headings and icons. Headings are in Outfit and end with a full stop, body text is in Inter. Buttons and the tab bar are pill shaped, and the plates overlap their cards.

projects.title: CineNebula
projects.blurb: CineNebula is a streaming service concept: a featured title screen for a film and series platform, designed for desktop and mobile. It started as a personal project to sharpen prototyping skills.
projects.meta: Concept project, 2026. UI design, prototyping and responsive design.
projects.overview: CineNebula is a streaming service concept: a featured title screen for a film and series platform, designed for desktop and mobile. It started as a personal project to sharpen prototyping skills.

sections.heading: Design
sections.text: One title fills the first screen, with its artwork, likes, year, genre and age rating. Season and episode dropdowns, Play Now and My Wishlist sit beside it, and a row of other titles runs along the bottom.

sections.heading: Visual language
sections.text: A near black background with a deep green glow rising from the bottom, and one brighter green saved for the likes rating. Text is white Outfit, and the buttons and dropdowns use the same dark green.

sections.heading: Mobile
sections.text: On a phone the same content stacks up. The artwork comes first, a menu button and search bar replace the navigation links, and the season and episode selectors share a row.

projects.title: Kairo Website
projects.blurb: Kairo Design Bureau needed a home of its own, a site that shows how the studio thinks before anyone reads a word.
projects.meta: Kairo Design Bureau, 2026. Web design, motion and development.
projects.overview: Kairo Design Bureau needed a home of its own, a site that shows how the studio thinks before anyone reads a word. We designed and built it ourselves between 23 September and 7 October 2026. It has one scrolling homepage, three discipline pages and a case study template, and it runs on GitHub Pages.

sections.heading: The brief
sections.text: The brief was short: minimal, premium, easy to navigate, motion that follows the scroll, and five brand colours. Two rules shaped the rest. The site had to run as plain files on GitHub Pages with no build step, so the studio can update it from a browser. And nothing could be made up: no stock photos, no placeholder clients, no invented numbers.

sections.heading: How we worked
sections.text: We skipped static mock-ups and designed in the browser. Each round went the same way: publish a working preview, open it on a desktop and a phone, change only what was flagged, upload. The copy was edited straight on the live preview. We kept the design system small on purpose: charcoal with one gold accent per screen, Inter Tight for headlines, Inter for text, square edges, hairline rules and a single easing curve for every movement.

sections.heading: The hero
sections.text: The first idea was a real-time 3D bowerbird that follows the cursor. For launch we went with something lighter that does the same job: a film of the character that breathes while you're on the first screen and closes its eyes as you scroll away. On desktop, scrolling scrubs through a video. iPhones wouldn't repaint a video while it was being scrubbed, so phones play the same film from 121 still frames packed into two files.

sections.heading: Where it landed
sections.text: Testing on real devices turned up two problems. The page sometimes opened part-way down, and the hero froze on iPhone. Both are fixed. After that came the work pages. Each discipline has its own page, and every case study uses one template fed by a single data file, so adding a project just means adding some text and a folder of images. The site is live, and the studio's first client projects are already on it.
